name: Suruwaha
confidence_why: Everett 1996 and Suzuki 1997 both place main stress on the final syllable of every word, and they differ only on secondary stress (alternating from the right in Everett 1996, always on the first syllable in Suzuki 1997), so the final-stress record rests on two descriptions that agree on the main stress but share a fieldwork lineage.

A sílaba tônica sempre vem acompanhada de tom alto.' [haːˈbu] 'carrapato', [kaʃinʲaˈri] 'tipo de planta'. p.81: 'A acentuação secundária é sempre observada na primeira sílaba da palavra.' [ˌaːmaˈsa] 'muito', [ˌharakaˈdɨ] 'arco'. 'O sistema iâmbico é válido para a acentuação primária, mas não serve para a acentuação secundária. Ao se observar a acentuação secundária em palavras de quatro sílabas pode se notar um sistema trocaico.' [ˌkarakuˈwɨ] 'nojo', [ˌmakahaˈra], [ˌawabiˈdʒa]. p.82: 'Um pé trocaico, responsável pela acentuação secundária (sendo a sílaba acentuada o troqueu mais à esquerda) seguido de um pé iâmbico, responsável pela acentuação primária.'
new_statements.translation: p.80: 'The stressed syllable in Suruwaha is always the last syllable of the word and has a demarcative function. One of the acoustic criteria that helps in perceiving this syllable is tone. The stressed syllable is always accompanied by high tone.' p.81: 'Secondary stress is always observed on the first syllable of the word.' 'The iambic system is valid for primary stress, but does not work for secondary stress. When one observes secondary stress in four-syllable words a trochaic system can be seen.' p.82: 'A trochaic foot, responsible for secondary stress (the stressed syllable being the leftmost trochee), followed by an iambic foot, responsible for primary stress.'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress always falls on the final syllable of the word (demarcative, carried by high tone). Secondary stress always falls on the first syllable of the word; in four-syllable words this gives initial + final (1001), which the author analyses as one left-headed (trochaic) foot at the left edge followed by one right-headed (iambic) foot at the right edge, feet being bimoraic. Section 4.3 adds that the first-syllable vowel of bi- and trisyllabic words is lengthened and carries a high-to-low falling tone, which the author treats as the melodic correlate of secondary accent; words of more than three syllables show the falling tone on syllable 1 without clear lengthening.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicitly described: 'sempre observada na primeira sílaba da palavra' (always on the first syllable), p.81; 4-syllable examples [ˌkarakuˈwɨ], [ˌmakahaˈra], [ˌawabiˈdʒa] (1001) and the 5-syllable name [ˌdʒadawaˈbu]/[ˌdʒadaaˈbu] (p.83, 4 syllables in slow register, 1001). The author explicitly rejects the iambic (0101) secondary pattern of Suzuki (1995a) and Everett (1995) for these words, arguing that the second syllable is unstressed because syllables with [h]/[r] onset delete in unstressed position ([ˌharakaˈdɨ] > [ˌhaːrkaˈdɨ]); 'Se a segunda sílaba fosse realmente acentuada ela não sofreria o processo de apagamento silábico.' No examples of 5+-syllable words in the stress section.
new_statements.exceptions: p.80-81: the proper name [dʒadaːbu] appears to have stress on [da], but the author explains it as compensatory lengthening of the second syllable after contraction of [dʒadaˈwa-bu] 'seja gente', the final syllable still carrying the highest tone; so no genuine exception to final primary stress is admitted.
new_statements.identity_note: Suzuki 1997 describes the Suruwaha of the single community on the Igarapé Coxodoá (Cunhuá/Riozinho basin, município de Tapauá, Amazonas; ~140 people), which he says formed from seven earlier groups that spoke a common language with some differences (p. 84); a few older speakers retain group-specific habits (e.g. one man labializes all consonants after [u]), but no dialectal variation in stress is reported. Corpus: ~2500 words collected in the area, transcribed in formal register, with examples recorded in CECIL for acoustic analysis (intro). The listed citation gives the year as 1977; the thesis itself is dated 1997 (Unicamp/IEL, advisor M. B. Abaurre), so the MPG record's date is a typo for the same work.

readall_conflicts: One disagreement, on secondary stress only. The catalog record (StressTyp2, derived from Everett 1996's right-to-left iambic analysis, alternating stress from the right) predicts 0101 in four-syllable words. Suzuki 1997 (sec. 4.2, pp. 81-82) states that secondary stress is always on the first syllable and cites four-syllable words [ˌkarakuˈwɨ], [ˌmakahaˈra], [ˌawabiˈdʒa] (1001), explicitly rejecting the iambic secondary-stress account of Suzuki 1995a and Everett 1995 on the grounds that second syllables with [h]/[r] onsets delete in fast speech and therefore cannot be stressed. Both sources agree that primary stress is always word-final. The disagreement is between two descriptions of the same community by people who worked from the same data (Everett's Suruwaha data come from the Suzukis), so it is an analytic dispute, not a dialect difference; the catalog's alternating pattern for 5+-syllable words rests on Everett alone and Suzuki 1997 offers no 5+-syllable examples.

At minimum add Suzuki 1997 sec. 4.2 to 'contra' and mark the secondary-stress pattern as disputed between the two primary sources; resolve with Huber Azevedo 2024 when obtained.
